correctness.rationale: For each row a, every component on ker(A^T A)=ker A is zero. Each distinct positive eigenspace therefore contributes one simple pole with numerator equal to the squared norm of the projected row. Combining the q poles gives a polynomial of degree at most q−1 over a denominator positive for λ>0; the identically zero numerator is a separate case, and a simple positive zero changes sign. For sharpness, let P and Q be the prescribed monic numerator and pole denominator. Evaluating the cleared rational identity at −d_k gives residues P(−d_k)/Q'(−d_k); both sides of the cleared identity have degree ≤q−1 and agree at q points. Split the residues divided by d_k into positive and negative parts, scale by ε and take square roots to obtain the first two rows x and y of U. The frozen strict bound on ε makes I−xx^T−yy^T positive definite. Its square root completes U to q orthonormal columns with q+2 rows, so A=U diag(sqrt(d_k)) has the required spectrum and the required difference of two scores for that same A. This covers repeated positive modes in the upper bound, q=1, and the rank-deficient case, without using λ=0. In the frozen three-mode example the mass of the two rows is 28/45 and the signed residues are (5,−18,14)/30, giving the two stated simple crossings. The separate replay `python /workspace/review_checks/frozen_probes.py` checks that identity at rational points and an exact alternative two-mode isometry crossing at λ=2. No frozen checker was executed.

value.rationale: Score-based deterministic selection motivates an exact question: can a ranking obtained at one penalty be reused as the penalty varies? The sharp bound depends on spectral diversity rather than row count. The thin common-matrix realization provides an explicit obstruction to assuming even a single reversal, or that reversal locations are constrained once a singular spectrum is fixed. That converse, not just counting polynomial zeros, gives a usable exact boundary. No whole-sort, runtime, or statistical improvement is inferred.
